StoryText: Grandma is getting old. She always craves that taste from her childhood. She took out an old, yellowed cookbook from the bottom of her suitcase, intending to recreate that childhood taste according to the steps in the cookbook. However, due to the passage of time, the words on the cookbook were no longer legible.

The first stop begins on an old arcade street.\nIn her hand is a small bag of rice, and in the recipe book only one warning remains: rice can turn burnt under the wrong pressure.\nShe starts with the simplest flavor: a clean grain memory.

After the rice returns as soft powder, a brittle tea leaf slips from the next page.\nTea is different. Its bitterness arrives first, and sweetness follows only with patience.\nGrandma sits by the window and listens for the rhythm of the leaves.

At the next market stop, Grandma weighs beans against sweetness while an old citrus scent lingers nearby.\nThe faded recipe no longer says how each flavor should enter.\nShe must recover the dessert by remembering what comes first, what follows, and what waits until the end.

Inside a wooden spice cabinet, Grandma finds peanut and black sesame stored in separate compartments.\nTheir roasted aromas belong together, but each needs room to keep its own character.\nShe opens the recipe book and prepares to restore the crisp one batch at a time.

Three sharp aromas wait behind a blue curtain: white pepper, ginger, and dried tangerine peel.\nThe old notes suggest that two once worked side by side while the third kept its distance.\nGrandma studies the little bags and searches for the blend hidden between them.

At a roadside stall, Grandma recalls a paste that was dark and fragrant, yet never harsh.\nBlack sesame gave it depth, while glutinous rice softened every spoonful.\nThe memory will return only if strength and gentleness meet in the right balance.

By the water, Grandma gathers the next fragments of a bold seasoning memory.\nSand ginger must carry the flavor, while familiar citrus and salt remain quiet companions.\nShe turns back to the mortar, ready to find how much support a strong base truly needs.

Along the harbor shelves, familiar ingredients appear in a new arrangement.\nPepper, peanut, and dried peel each remember a different touch and rhythm.\nGrandma knows this recipe cannot be rushed together; every ingredient must first tell its own story.

At the final stall, Grandma gathers familiar filling ingredients and a broad lotus leaf.\nThe grains and roasted flavors must become one memory before the leaf can close around them.\nShe recalls that wrapping is the last gesture, not another ingredient to grind away.

At the harbor, Grandma finds the deep savory aroma of Yangjiang douchi.\nGinger, dried tangerine peel, and coarse salt wait nearby, each carrying a lesson from an earlier page.\nShe opens the cookbook again and begins to rebuild the savory base.

The next page brings together two familiar gingers and a fresh scallion stem.\nThe ginger pair must form the bold first layer, while scallion stem stays fresh in its own batch.\nA little coarse salt will finish the sauce only after every layer is ready.

On the final recipe page, Yangjiang douchi meets ginger, scallion stem, and coarse salt.\nThe savory base leads, the fresh scallion waits separately, and the smallest finishing note comes last.\nGrandma gathers every lesson from the Experiment Log for one last taste to restore.
